To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV prevention approaches for Muslim communities must be based on a sound theoretical foundation and must incorporate the Islamic concept of jihad.

(1) HIV prevalence rates among Muslims are increasing; (2) Muslim populations have been largely ignored in HIV prevention efforts; and (3) the concept of jihad can serve as an important tool for HIV prevention.

HIV prevalence rates are increasing among Muslim populations due to unprotected sexual activity and shared injection equipment and that HIV prevention programs that target Muslim populations should be based on HIV prevention theory and integrate the important Islamic concept jihad.

the development of a culturally and spiritually grounded HIV prevention approach that can be used to reduce HIV infection in Muslim populations.
how the Islamic concept of jihad can help Muslims to reduce HIV risk and how HIV prevention can be integrated with the Islamic concept of struggle.

there is no evidence to support the idea that Muslims are less likely to be infected by HIV than non-Muslims.

we have demonstrated that the Islamic concept of jihad is a useful theoretical framework for HIV prevention in Muslim populations and that the theory of reasoned action is a useful theoretical approach for HIV prevention in any population.
